episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Cariboo Local Affairs
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Cariboo Local Affairs.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: When is small genuinely better, and when is it just an excuse?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Eby promises gas tax cut, price caps at the pumps if NDP is re-elected and Carney designates proposed Alberta to B.C. pipeline a project of national interest, plus 11 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Does small-town governance deliver better accountability through proximity, or does it fail due to insufficient staff capacity and public scrutiny? Topics include: Mayoral accountability and voter behavior in the 2018 and 2022 Williams Lake elections, Council candidate diversity and the significance of eight first-time candidates versus established candidates with known records, Regional district acclamations in Areas D and F and the lack of public scrutiny for unopposed positions, Scott Nelson's unresolved business lawsuit and the absence of an integrity commissioner in small-town governance, The role of local media (Tribune) and the conflict of interest when a reporter becomes a candidate, School board trustee Michael Franklin running unopposed and the challenge of evaluating single candidates.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Salvation Army Williams Lake

discussion.central_question: Does small-town governance deliver better accountability through proximity, or does it fail due to insufficient staff capacity and public scrutiny?
discussion.riley_position: Small towns can be accountable because voters know their candidates and have demonstrated willingness to remove incumbents; a large field of newcomers shows the pipeline of willing candidates is open, not a sign of a captured system.
riley_key_evidence: Walt Cobb won the 2018 mayoral race with 60.4% of the vote but finished third in 2022 when Rathor won with 34.1%, showing voters will punish underperforming incumbents
In 2022 Williams Lake had four serious mayoral candidates, and council had fourteen candidates running, demonstrating public engagement
Leaders and involved candidates like Sheldon Clare and Doerkson show up in their ridings and need strong margins to win
discussion.casey_position: Small-town accountability is illusory without external oversight; the public record is too thin to evaluate most candidates, acclaimed positions face no scrutiny, and without a professional press or integrity infrastructure, small size merely means insular decision-making.
casey_key_evidence: Michael Franklin runs unopposed for the school board trustee seat, Steve Forseth and Maureen LeBourdais were both acclaimed as regional directors with no record publicly available

Scott Nelson, a council candidate, faces a June 2025 B.C. Supreme Court petition alleging breach of fiduciary duty and misappropriated funds, with a consent order in August 2025, yet a small council has no integrity commissioner to investigate
Surinderpal Rathor's record as mayor has not been established from available sources; his own Facebook lists seven council terms from 1993-2014 but his actual mayoral accomplishments are undocumented
discussion.resolution: The debaters agreed they lack sufficient information but identified a concrete test: asking each candidate and the city to publicly list deferred projects and priorities that couldn't be completed due to staff constraints, which would reveal whether capacity limits are tracked and what they actually mean in practice.
topics_covered: Mayoral accountability and voter behavior in the 2018 and 2022 Williams Lake elections
Council candidate diversity and the significance of eight first-time candidates versus established candidates with known records
Regional district acclamations in Areas D and F and the lack of public scrutiny for unopposed positions
Scott Nelson's unresolved business lawsuit and the absence of an integrity commissioner in small-town governance

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

**Scope note.** I could not read the Elections BC PDF, because it came back as garbled text. I also ran out of page reads before the Tribune's Sept. 15 CRD story and the Oct. 1 NDP release. Most of the records below come from search snippets and the pages I did read.

---

**RESEARCH QUESTION: Williams Lake mayor's race (Rathor vs. Cobb)**

Findings:
- **Filing.** The Williams Lake Tribune (Sept. 12, 2026) reported that two candidates filed for mayor: incumbent Surinderpal Rathor and former mayor Walt Cobb.
- **Rathor's 2022 win.**
  - CFJC (Oct. 15, 2022) reported preliminary results with Rathor at 34.1% of the vote.
  - He beat councillor Jason Ryll (28.1%), incumbent mayor Walt Cobb (24.2%) and former mayor Kerry Cook (13.4%).
  - The Tribune's preliminary count was Rathor 1,091, Ryll 898 and Cobb 773.
- **Rathor's earlier record.**
  - His Facebook page says he was on council for seven terms, from 1993 to 2014. That is self-described.
  - The city staff directory says he was elected mayor in 2022 and is the first Indo-Canadian mayor of Williams Lake.
  - The same Tribune live blog lists a 2018 mayoral result: Cobb 1,843 votes (60.4%) to Rathor's 1,177. That means Rathor lost a mayoral run in 2018 and then won in 2022.
- **Cobb's record.**
  - He lost his seat as the incumbent in 2022, finishing third.
  - FPAC says he was a city councillor from 1980 to 1990 and mayor from 1990 to 1996.
  - Wikipedia says he was a BC Liberal MLA for Cariboo South from 2001 to 2005.
  - The CBC (Nov. 1, 2021) reported he was mayor "since 2014" and was re-elected in 2018.
- **Cobb's controversy (CBC, Nov. 1, 2021).**
  - Williams Lake First Nation Chief Willie Sellars called for Cobb to resign after Cobb shared a Facebook post. The post claimed there were positive aspects of residential schools and that young Indigenous people "just want to be victims."
  - Cobb told the Tribune he shared a forwarded post and said "we need to look at every side of everything." The post was deleted.
  - This was a call for resignation, not a finding. I did not establish the council outcome, so the show should not state one.
- **Rathor's record in office.** I found nothing on his council votes or any controversy. Two My Cariboo Now pieces carry his "second term, keep the momentum" pitch, but I did not read them.

Suggested angle: Riley can argue this is a rematch of a race Cobb lost. Casey can press on what Cobb's 2021 episode and his third-place 2022 finish say about whether he has a comeback case.

---

**RESEARCH QUESTION: Williams Lake council: incumbents and returning candidates**

Findings:
- **Scott Nelson (incumbent).**
  - The city directory says he has served about 20 years on council and was mayor for three years.
  - Victoria News/Williams Lake Tribune (Ruth Lloyd, Aug. 27, 2025) reported a B.C. Supreme Court petition filed June 25, 2025. It was brought by Dr. Mark Lambiotte Inc., Dr. J.D. Neufeld Inc. and members of the Lambiotte family against Nelson, his wife Twila Smigelsky and their companies.
  - The petition alleges breaches of fiduciary duty, forged signatures and misappropriation of funds. It says as much as $15 million in refinancing and sale proceeds went unaccounted for. **These are allegations, and "none of the accusations have been proven in court."**
  - Nelson's lawyer, Patrick Sullivan, said the claims are "fundamentally wrong" and called it a dispute between business partners.
  - A consent order in early August 2025 restrained the couple from moving assets of the named companies.
  - The article also mentions an earlier case in which Nelson and a business partner split co-owned rental properties.
  - I did not find the current status of the case.
  - Nelson's Tribune profile describes a bid for a third consecutive term. I did not see that profile's date.
  - My Cariboo Now covered a Nelson notice of motion on an "aggressive" stance on prolific offenders. I did not see the date or whether the motion passed.
- **Sheila Boehm (incumbent).**
  - A chiropractor, and a two-term School District 27 trustee before council, per the Tribune.
  - Her Tribune profile describes a second council term. I found no controversy and no vote record.
- **Michael Moses (incumbent).**
  - The Tribune (Sept. 5, 2026) said he was first elected in 2022 with support from Indigenous leadership.
  - The city directory describes him as Secwépemc and Nlaka'pamux and says he is a Canadian Mental Health Association Cariboo Chilcotin board member (his X bio says president).
  - I found no vote record or controversy.
- **Jason Ryll.**
  - The Tribune (Sept. 4, 2026) said he filed for mayor four years ago. That matches the 2022 result: he finished second, with 28.1% per CFJC.
  - The Tribune (Sept. 12) and CivicInfoBC say he served on council before 2022. He was a sitting councillor when he ran for mayor in 2022.
  - My Cariboo Now (Sept. 4) says he is general manager of Vista Radio in the Cariboo.
  - The Tribune (Sept. 4) calls him a former councillor, so he apparently did not return to council in 2022. I did not confirm his council terms or whether he ran for council that year.
- **Paul French.**
  - The Tribune (Sept. 12) says he previously served on council before 2022, per CivicInfoBC. His terms and past results are not established.
  - The Tribune (Apr. 29, 2026) calls him past president of the Williams Lake and District Chamber of Commerce.
  - A CBC story identifies a Paul French as first vice-president of United Steelworkers Local 1-2017. I could not confirm it is the same person, so the show should not assert it.
- **Ruth Lloyd.**
  - The Tribune (Sept. 12) calls her a former Tribune journalist and a newcomer.
  - The Tribune (Dec. 30, 2025; Jan. 3, 2026) ran letters supporting her after a city councillor questioned one of her articles in a social media video. The councillor is not named in what I saw. The city then issued a letter saying individual councillors' comments do not necessarily reflect council's position.
  - Lloyd also wrote the Aug. 2025 Nelson lawsuit story. Hosts should flag that she is both the reporter on that story and a candidate now, and they should not link it to the councillor's video unless a source does.
  - I did not establish when she left the Tribune.
- **Newcomers.**
  - Whitney Spearing: director of natural resources at Williams Lake First Nation, and an archaeologist (RocketReach and ZoomInfo; SFU profile; Tribune video on the Stampede Grounds heritage park).
  - Rafiullah Sahibzada: the Tribune (Aug. 1, 2026) calls him a member of the Muslim community. He appeared before council on June 16, 2026 with Central Cariboo Islamic Center members on safety concerns (Today in BC, June 30, 2026). He moved to Williams Lake in 2019 (Tribune, July 16, 2026).
  - Billie Sheridan: the Tribune (June 4, 2026) reported her as an openly transgender woman, and said Williams Lake could have its first openly trans councillor. The Agassiz-Harrison Observer describes her as a Williams Lake Pride Society organizer who criticized a bill Lorne Doerkson voted to bring to debate. That is a date-unverified link to the provincial race.
  - Cianna O'Connor: listed in the Williams Lake Studio Theatre member directory, but a different person appears in other results. I could not confirm it is the same person.
  - Kayla Zaruk: a 2024 Tribune piece lists her with a Tŝilhqot'in National Government email on an awareness course. A LinkedIn profile shows a dental clinic role. I could not confirm which is current.
- **Withdrawal.** Jared Wardlaw-Gimbel withdrew, so the hosts should not describe him as running.

Suggested angle: Casey can ask how voters weigh the Nelson lawsuit, which is unproven and denied, against 20 years of incumbency. Riley can point to the number of first-time candidates as a sign of renewal.

---

**RESEARCH QUESTION: Cariboo Regional District, Areas D, E and F, and School District 27 Zone 6**

Findings:
- **Area D, Steve Forseth.**
  - Acclaimed (Williams Lake Tribune, Sept. 15, 2026), so voters get no ballot for this seat.
  - The Tribune (June 16, 2026) reported he was running again.
  - The Tribune reports he was NCLGA first vice-president and later president. I did not see the dates.
  - I found no controversy.
- **Area F, Maureen LeBourdais.**
  - Acclaimed (Tribune, Sept. 15, 2026), so voters get no ballot for this seat.
  - The Tribune headline says "CRD byelection," and CKPG (Sept. 30, 2020) shows her as Area F director. That suggests she first won in a by-election, but the date is not established.
  - A Tribune profile says she is a long-time Beaver Valley resident. A 2023 Tribune piece shows her selling weaving at the Horsefly market.
  - I found no controversy.
- **Area E, Neufeld vs. Forbes.**
  - Tribune, Sept. 15, 2026: Melynda Neufeld is the incumbent, challenged by Mary Forbes. Prince George Daily News (Sept. 22, 2026) confirms both names.
  - The Tribune says Neufeld has been director since 2022 and board vice-chair since Nov. 2023.
  - An older My Cariboo Now item lists "Angie Delainey and Melynda Neufeld" for Area E. The year is not shown, but it is probably the 2022 contest. I did not confirm who won or by what margin.
  - Mary Forbes: the BC Achievement Foundation credits her with leading the Potato House Project in Williams Lake, a heritage home restoration. Love Northern BC lists a Mary Forbes as a Dandelion Tours interpreter. I have not confirmed these are the same person as the candidate, so the show should not merge them.
  - Elections BC's registered-candidates PDF lists a Mary Forbes at an Esler Road address. I could not confirm that is her.
  - I found no previous run for Forbes, no platform for either candidate, and no controversy.
- **SD27 Zone 6, Michael Franklin.**
  - The Tribune (Sept. 14, 2026) says he is the current board member seeking re-election. He is the only candidate for the Zone 6 trustee seat.
  - Because he is unopposed, the show should not frame this as a contest.
  - A My Cariboo Now item names a Michael Franklin as Foundry Cariboo-Chilcotin manager. It is not confirmed to be the same person.
  - I found no vote record or controversy, and no first-elected year.
- **Other CRD note.** Besides Areas D and F, the Tribune lists Areas A, I and J incumbents as acclaimed.

Suggested angle: Casey can argue that two acclamations and an unopposed trustee mean many residents have no say at all. Riley can reply that acclamation can signal satisfaction, though I found no evidence either way.

---

**RESEARCH QUESTION: Cariboo-Chilcotin provincial riding**

Findings:
- **Lorne Doerkson.**
  - Incumbent, and now interim B.C. Conservative leader. Globe and Mail (Sept. 26, 2026) and CBC report he took over the leadership.
  - CBC and Global say he was first elected in 2020 as a B.C. Liberal, and the party later rebranded as B.C. United. He then crossed the floor to the Conservatives.
  - bcballot.ca says he won Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2024 by 7,722 votes. Treat that margin as secondary-source.
  - My Cariboo Now covered his campaign promise to double LNG production by 2032.
  - The Agassiz-Harrison Observer says he voted to consider debating Bill M216, the Protecting Minors from Gender Transition Act. The article is date-unverified and should be checked.
- **Kathryn Askew (BC NDP).**
  - The Williams Lake Tribune (Oct. 1, 2026) named her the NDP candidate.
  - She is a retired schoolteacher from Canim Lake with 32 years in education. She held leadership roles with the BC Teachers' Federation and her local union, including local president and bargaining chair.
  - The Tribune says she volunteers with the Hawkins Lake volunteer fire department, the Forest Grove Legion and the Canim Lake Community Club.
  - The Tribune did not report a previous run for office.
- **Other parties.** I did not establish Green, Liberal or other candidates. bcballot.ca snippets list names like AJ Wolfe (OneBC) and Pete Davis, but the riding attribution is unclear, so do not use them.

Suggested angle: Doerkson is the party leader and so is campaigning province-wide while defending his own seat. Casey can ask what that means for local attention.

---

**RESEARCH QUESTION: Prince George-North Cariboo (includes Quesnel)**

Findings:
- **Sheldon Clare.**
  - The Elections BC candidate report shows him as the Conservative candidate. The Prince George Citizen says he is on the ballot.
  - The Conservative Party site says he is seeking re-election.
  - CFJC (Feb. 28, 2026) reported he suspended his B.C. Conservative leadership bid. CTV and the Times Colonist reported he declared for the leadership earlier, saying he wanted to stop former provincial Liberals from regaining control of the party.
  - The Wikipedia entry says he was deputy whip in the Conservative caucus. My Cariboo Now (Nov. 21, 2024) is cited for that.
  - My Cariboo Now has an article titled "Conservative candidate Sheldon Clare clears the air on the past 48 hours." I could not read it, so the controversy is unknown. The date is also unclear.
- **Opponents.** I did not establish an NDP, Green or other candidate for 2026. The My Cariboo Now item naming Denice Bardua and Randy Thompson, with Independent Coralee Oakes as incumbent, is from the 2017 election and should not be used.
- **The 2024 win.** Elections BC (Oct. 19, 2024) reported Clare winning for the Conservatives. I did not establish the margin.

Suggested angle: As a former leadership hopeful who is back as a rank-and-file candidate, Clare gives Casey an angle on how settled the Conservatives are going into the vote.

---

**Other context.** The My Cariboo Now item says the major parties were close to full slates across all 93 ridings the day before the Oct. 3 deadline. Dates: the provincial election is Oct. 24; local elections are Oct. 17.

NO RECORD FOUND: Charlene Hays; Greg Jeannotte; Cianna O'Connor; Nathan Wiebe; Mary Forbes (prior runs and platform); Kayla Zaruk (current role); Walt Cobb and Surinderpal Rathor (any council-vote record); Michael Franklin (record as trustee); Maureen LeBourdais (record in office); Steve Forseth (record in office); Kathryn Askew (prior runs); any 2026 opponent to Sheldon Clare; any Green or other opponent to Lorne Doerkson
